title: 10 People Who Backed AI Breakouts, and How to Find Your Version
summary: 10 People Who Backed AI Breakouts, and How to Find Your Version
body_markdown:
A founder raising money for an AI company can get an introduction to someone who likes AI. That's a start, but it doesn't say much. If you're building a tool for accountants, the more useful investor might be the one who knows why an accountant won't let a model send an answer without checking it first.


Funding announcements are useful because they show who was on the other side of an actual decision. The names below are historical. A named participant may have invested personally or through a vehicle, and the announcement doesn't tell us what they wrote, whether they take pitches now, or whether they'll back a competitor. What it gives us is a good place to start asking questions.


## Four companies, ten disclosed backers


- [Cursor, Series A](https://cursor.com/blog/series-a) : Jeff Dean and Noam Brown. A coding tool sits at the intersection of engineering systems and how well a model can work through a hard problem. Look for people who have built or evaluated either half.
- [ElevenLabs, Series A](https://elevenlabs.io/blog/elevenlabs-launches-new-generative-voice-ai-products-and-announces-19m-series-a-round-led-by-nat-friedman-daniel-gross-and-andreessen-horowitz) : Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross were named co-leads. Mike Krieger and Anjney Midha were named strategic angels. A voice product needs good model output; it also needs someone to want to use it a second time. That's a performance problem and a product problem.
- [Perplexity, seed](https://www.perplexity.ai/es/hub/blog/announcing-our-series-a-funding-round-and-mobile-app-launch) : Andrej Karpathy and Amjad Masad were named in the company's account of its seed round, published when it announced its Series A. For a product whose usefulness depends on whether users trust its answers, the combination of model expertise and experience making technical tools easier to use is worth studying.
- [Mercor, Series A](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/mercor-raises-30m-series-a-at-a-250m-valuation-to-create-jobs-with-ai-302252449.html) : Adam D’Angelo and Jack Dorsey were named participants. If your product connects people to work, operating a marketplace or a product built around user contributions may be more relevant experience than investing in your category last month.


Those observations are our reading of the fit. The companies didn't necessarily choose these people for those reasons. That's an important difference when you make your own list.


## Pick the investor for the problem you'll actually have


Write down the objection likely to sink your next ten sales calls. It might be accuracy, cost, data access, or the time it takes to deploy. Then list three people who have solved a similar problem, not three people who show up on podcasts about AI. Look for one public piece of evidence for each person. An early round in a comparable company is good. An essay describing how they solved the problem may be better.


Start with the person one step away from the famous example. A former engineering lead who shipped the kind of system you're building can be easier to reach, and perhaps even more useful, than the company’s best-known investor. Send the smallest demonstration that shows something difficult working. Ask one question you would value having answered even if they never invested.


Keep each lead's role, public source, stage, and your reason for contacting them in a sheet. Leave check size blank until someone tells you. That's a better starting point than a directory full of precise numbers nobody has verified.
